output.answer: I understand you want to be with your parents for the birth, and that's a very natural wish. However, I would strongly advise against taking an overnight bus journey at 36 weeks. The passages I have highlight that complications can develop at any time and are not always predictable (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27). A long journey puts you far from a health facility if an emergency arises, like premature rupture of membranes or the start of pre-term labour, which is defined as labour before 37 weeks (MOHFW-ANC, p. 81). If you were to go into labour on the bus, you would not have the skilled care, equipment, or a referral system that a facility provides to keep you and your baby safe (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27). Please discuss your travel plans with your doctor. They can assess your specific situation and help you make the safest plan for your delivery.

/circle6 Some women experience a decreased desire for sex during pregnancy. Th  e husband 
should be informed that this is normal and the woman's consent should be sought 
before engaging in sex.
/circle6 Some couples fi  nd engaging in sex uncomfortable during pregnancy. Th e husband must 
see to the comfort of the woman while engaging in sexual activities.
/circle6 Advice couples to have safe sex and use condoms especially if the woman has discharge 
or itching in the vaginal area or the husband has urethral discharge or experiences 
burning while urinating.
/circle6 Th  e couple should be advised to abstain from having sex during the fi rst six weeks post-
partum or longer if the perineal wounds have not healed by then.
F. Domestic violence 
Pregnancy should be a time of peace and safety, but for many women it can be a time when 
they face violence. According to  the National Family Health Survey  III (2005-6), in India 
39.7% of ever married women suff er from either physical and/or sexual violence. Domestic 
abuse and violence against pregnant women has immediate and lasting eff ects both on the 
pregnant woman and the foetus. Some of the complications might be visible directly, such 
as blunt trauma to the abdomen, haemorrhage (including placental separation), uterine 
rupture, miscarriage/still birth, pre-term labour and PROM, all of which need to be ruled 
out.

Communication and genuine empathy are probably the 
most important components of eff ective care in such situations.
At the time of the event
/circle6 Listen to those who are distressed. Th e family/woman will need to discuss their hurt and 
sorrow.
/circle6 Do not change the subject or move on to easier or less painful topics of conversation. 
Show empathy.
/circle6 Tell the family/woman as much as you can and as much as they can understand about 
what is happening. Understanding the situation and its management can reduce their 
anxiety and prepare them for what happens next.

/circle6 Be honest. Do not hesitate to admit what you do not know. Maintaining trust matters 
more than appearing knowledgeable.
/circle6 If language/dialect is a barrier to communication identify someone to translate 
for you. 
Aft er the event
/circle6 Give practical assistance, information and emotional support.
/circle6 Respect traditional beliefs and customs, and accommodate the family’s needs as far as 
possible.
/circle6 Explain the problem to help reduce anxiety and guilt. Repeat information several times 
and give written information, if possible. People going through an emergency will not 
remember much of what is said to them.
/circle6 Many families and women blame themselves for what has happened. Counsel the family 
and woman and allow them to refl ect on the event.
/circle6 Listen and express understanding and acceptance of the woman’s feelings. Non-verbal 
communication may speak louder than words: a touch of the hand or a look of concern 
can say an enormous amount. 
/circle6 Y ou yourself may feel anger, guilt, sorrow, pain and frustration in the face of obstetric 
emergencies that may lead you to avoid talking to the family/woman. Remember, 
expressing your emotions is not a weakness.

T able 1. WHO recommendation on imaging ultrasound before 24 weeks of pregnancy 
One ultrasound scan before 24 weeks of gestation is recommended for pregnant women to 
estimate gestational age, improve detection of fetal anomalies and multiple pregnancies, reduce 
induction of labour for post-term pregnancy, and improve a woman’s pregnancy experience.
Remarks
• The evidence on effects of routine imaging ultrasound before 24 weeks of pregnancy has not changed 
materially since the 2016 recommendation. A newly identified large-cluster randomized controlled trial 
(RCT) conducted in low-resource settings was reviewed but was not found suitable for inclusion in meta-
analysis, because it evaluated the effect of two imaging ultrasounds conducted in both the second and 
third trimesters (i.e. it did not address the guideline’s participants, intervention, comparator, outcome 
[PICO] question). 
• Implementation considerations associated with this recommendation have been significantly expanded 
based on the findings of a new qualitative evidence synthesis of the views and experiences of service users 
and health workers.a
• Ultrasound scan can guide subsequent care. When implementing or scaling up routine imaging ultrasound 
before 24 weeks of pregnancy, the purpose of imaging ultrasound should be to assess:
 – location of pregnancy (e.g. intrauterine)
 – cardiac activity
 – fetal size
 – gestational age
 – fetal number
 – chorionicity and amnionicity for multiple gestation.
• Where the skill set and health systems allow, the following, which are more informative after 18 weeks of 
pregnancy, may also be assessed:
 – presence of normal head, neck, face, spine, chest, heart, abdomen, abdominal wall and extremities
 – placental appearance and location, and umbilical cord.
• Those who perform obstetric ultrasound should have specialized training that is appropriate to the 
practice of screening ultrasound in pregnancy. 
• Many pregnancy complications, including fetal malformations, may develop later in pregnancy or may not 
be detectable without appropriate ultrasound training and equipment.
• There remain some uncertainties around undesirable effects, including the risk of litigation, the potential 
for female feticide, the short- and long-term psychological impact of an inconclusive or adverse scan 
finding, and the potential for overuse of ultrasound scans (as a replacement for formal ANC contacts).

1 Introduction
1.1 Background
An imaging ultrasound scan is widely used to estimate gestational age, investigate suspected pregnancy 
complications and monitor complicated pregnancies when they occur. In 2016, the World Health Organization 
(WHO) added a single ultrasound scan before 24 weeks of pregnancy to its list of recommended interventions 
for routine antenatal care (ANC) (1). In most high-income countries, routine antenatal ultrasound screening has 
been standard practice for some time, often being conducted in both the first and second trimesters (2). When 
conducted in the first trimester (up to and including 13 weeks and 6 days of gestation), an imaging ultrasound 
scan is aimed at confirming fetal viability, identifying the location of the gestational sac, establishing gestational 
age, determining the number of fetuses and, in the presence of a multiple pregnancy, assessing chorionicity and 
amnionicity; also, towards the end of the first trimester, nuchal translucency thickness is commonly measured 
in settings that offer screening for fetal chromosomal abnormalities (3). Second-trimester ultrasound scans 
conducted between 18 and 24 weeks allow for more detailed examination of fetal anatomy and detection of fetal 
anomalies, provide information on the number of fetuses present, identify the location of the placenta and enable 
an estimate of gestational age (4). 
A 2015 systematic review on ultrasound scans before 24 weeks of pregnancy (5) and a qualitative review on 
women’s views and experiences of pregnancy (6) informed the 2016 WHO recommendations on antenatal 
care for a positive pregnancy experience (1). The ultrasound recommendation (B2.4) is: “One ultrasound scan 
before 24 weeks of gestation (early ultrasound) is recommended for pregnant women to estimate gestational 
age, improve detection of fetal anomalies and multiple pregnancies, reduce induction of labour for post-
term pregnancy, and improve a woman’s pregnancy experience.” In the context of a new cluster-randomized 
randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluating the impact of routine ultrasound scans in low-resource settings (7), 
an independent Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) prioritized updating the 2016 recommendation. A new 
systematic review on routine ultrasound before 24 weeks of pregnancy has since been conducted (8).

It's completely normal to feel anxious about labour, and you don't have to just 'be happy.' The guidelines remind us that during labour, a woman goes through physical as well as mental trauma, and providing emotional support is a key part of care (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). Your feelings are valid. What you're experiencing is part of a 'positive pregnancy experience,' which includes woman-centred advice and treatment for common concerns (WHO-ANC, p. 74).

To help ease your mind, you can focus on what you can control. You have the right to choose the position you feel most comfortable in during labour (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). Knowing the signs of true labour, like regular contractions that increase in intensity, can also help you feel more prepared (MOHFW-ANC, p. 43).

Please talk to your doctor about your specific fears. They can walk you through what to expect and create a plan that respects your wishes. You are not alone in this.

Th e second stage of labour begins when the cervix is fully dilated and ends with the expulsion 
of the foetus. When the woman reaches this stage, she should be transferred to the labour 
room if she is in another room. She should not be allowed to walk during this stage.

WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
74
D. Interventions for common 
physiological symptoms
Background
Women’s bodies undergo substantial changes 
during pregnancy, which are brought about by both 
hormonal and mechanical effects. These changes lead 
to a variety of common symptoms – including nausea 
and vomiting, low back and pelvic pain, heartburn, 
varicose veins, constipation and leg cramps – that in 
some women cause severe discomfort and negatively 
affects their pregnancy experience. In general, 
symptoms associated with mechanical effects, e.g. 
pelvic pain, heartburn and varicose veins, often 
worsen as pregnancy progresses.
Symptoms of nausea and vomiting are experienced 
by approximately 70% of pregnant women and 
usually occur in the first trimester of pregnancy 
(156); however, approximately 20% of women may 
experience nausea and vomiting beyond 20 weeks of 
gestation (157). Low back and pelvic pain is estimated 
to occur in half of pregnant women, 8% of whom 
experience severe disability (158). Symptoms of 
heartburn occur in two thirds of pregnant women, 
and may be worse after eating and lying down (159). 
Varicose veins usually occur in the legs, but can also 
occur in the vulva and rectum, and may be associated 
with pain, night cramps, aching and heaviness, 
and worsen with long periods of standing (160). 
Constipation can be very troublesome and may be 
complicated by haemorrhoids (161). Leg cramps often 
occur at night and can be very painful, affecting sleep 
and daily activities (162). Suggested approaches to 
manage common physiological symptoms include a 
variety of non-pharmacological and pharmacological 
options and the GDG considered the evidence and 
other relevant information on these approaches.
Women’s values:
A scoping review of what women want from ANC 
and what outcomes they value informed the ANC 
guideline (13). Evidence showed that women from 
high-, medium- and low-resource settings valued 
having a positive pregnancy experience. This 
included woman-centred advice and treatment for 
common physiological symptoms (high confidence 
in the evidence).

WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
28
Maternal outcomes
High-certainty evidence shows that calcium 
supplementation does not have important effects 
on maternal anaemia (1 trial, 1098 women; RR: 
1.04, 95% CI: 0.90–1.22) or caesarean section rates 
(9 trials, 7440 women; RR: 0.99, 95% CI: 0.89–1.10). 
Moderate-certainty evidence indicates that calcium 
supplementation probably has little or no effect on 
maternal mortality (2 trials, 8974 women; RR: 0.29, 
95% CI: 0.06–1.38) and probably makes little or 
no difference to the risk of urinary tract infections 
(3 trials, 1743 women; RR: 0.95, 95% CI: 0.69–1.30). 
Low-certainty evidence suggests that calcium 
supplementation may make little or no difference 
to maternal weight gain (3 trials; MD: –29.46 g per 
week, 95% CI: –119.80 to 60.89 g per week). Maternal 
satisfaction was not reported in any of the trials 
included in the Cochrane review.
Side-effects: Calcium supplementation makes little 
or no difference to the risk of “any side-effect”, a 
composite outcome including headache, vomiting, 
backache, swelling, vaginal and urinary complaints, 
dyspepsia and abdominal pain (1 trial, 8312 women; 
RR: 1.02, 95% CI: 0.93–1.12), and probably makes little 
or no difference to the risk of urinary stones (3 trials, 
13 419 women; RR: 1.11, 95% CI: 0.48–2.54), renal colic 
(1 trial, 8312 women; RR: 1.67, 95% CI: 0.40–6.99) and 
impaired renal function (1 trial, 4589 women; RR: 0.91, 
95% CI: 0.51–1.64), all assessed as moderate-certainty 
evidence.

WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
54
B.2.1: Daily fetal movement counting
RECOMMENDATION B.2.1: Daily fetal movement counting, such as with “count-to-ten” 
kick charts, is only recommended in the context of rigorous research. (Context-specific 
recommendation – research)
Remarks
• Fetal movement counting is when a pregnant woman counts and records her baby’s movements in order 
to monitor the baby’s health. Various methods have been described, with further monitoring variously 
indicated depending on the method used, for example, if fewer than six distinct movements are felt within 
2 hours (115) or fewer than 10 distinct movements are felt within 12 hours (the Cardiff “count to ten” 
method) (106).
• While daily fetal movement counting is not recommended, healthy pregnant women should be made 
aware of the importance of fetal movements in the third trimester and of reporting reduced fetal 
movements. 
• Clinical enquiry by ANC providers at each ANC visit about maternal perception of fetal movements is 
recommended as part of good clinical practice. Women who perceive poor or reduced fetal movements 
require further monitoring (e.g. with daily fetal movement counting) and investigation, if indicated. 
• The GDG agreed that more research is needed on the effects of daily fetal movement counting in the third 
trimester of pregnancy, particularly in LMIC settings with a high prevalence of unexplained stillbirths.
Women’s values
A scoping review of what women want from ANC and what outcomes they value informed the ANC guideline (13). 
Evidence showed that women from high-, medium- and low-resource settings valued having a positive pregnancy 
experience. Within the context of maternal and fetal assessment, women valued the opportunity to receive screening 
and tests to optimize their health and that of their baby as long as individual procedures were explained to them 
clearly and administered by knowledgeable, supportive and respectful health-care practitioners (high confidence in 
the evidence).

Introduction 
Under-nutrition remains a pervasive issue for many women in India, with 
every third woman being undernourished and every second woman 
suffering from anaemia. This nutritional deficit often leads to an 
undernourished mother giving birth to a low birth weight baby, a condition 
that begins in -utero and whose largely irreversible effects can extend 
throughout the life cycle. Exacerbating these health challenges, economic 
and social distress compels many women to continue working right up to 
the advanced stages o f pregnancy and to prematurely resume work after 
childbirth. This sustained labour prevents their bodies from fully recovering 
and impedes their ability to exclusively breastfeed their infants during the 
crucial first six months. 
In response to these critical challenges, the Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana 
Yojana (PMMVY), a maternity benefit programme, was launched on the 1st 
January 2017. The scheme is implemented by the Ministry of Women and 
Child Development and forms a key component  of the Government of 
India's 'Mission Shakti' for women's empowerment.  
Under the 'Samarthya' sub -scheme, PMMVY focuses on economic 
empowerment and holistic development of women. It provides financial 
support to pregnant and lactating mothers under the National Food Security 
Act, 2013, to improve their health and nutrition and compensate for wage 
loss. In April 2022, PMMVY 2.0 extended maternity benefits for the second 
living child, if a girl, and to promote positive attitudes towards girls and 
improve the Sex Ratio at Birth . Mission Shakti guidelines support PMMVY 
2.0 implementation across national, state, and district levels.1

This is a delicate situation, and it’s wonderful that you’re seeking a way to support both your wife and your parents. The national guidelines strongly recommend an institutional delivery because complications can arise suddenly and unpredictably, and a health facility has the staff, equipment, and drugs to provide the best care for both mother and baby (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27).

Your wife’s preference for a hospital aligns with this safety advice. When speaking with your parents, you can gently explain that you respect their care and traditions, but your shared priority is the safest possible outcome. You can reassure them that your wife can still have supportive companionship during a hospital birth, which is encouraged to help her face fear and pain (MOHFW-ANC, p. 92).

A calm, united front with your wife will be your strongest approach. You are doing the right thing by focusing on her well-being and the baby’s safety.

It’s wonderful that you’re looking for ways to step in. While your wife recovers from a C-section, her body needs rest, and you can take on many night tasks to protect her sleep and healing.

Here are practical things you can do, based on what we know supports a positive postnatal experience:

*   **Bring the baby to her:** For night feeds, you can be the one to wake, pick up the baby, and bring them to your wife in bed. After the feed, you take over for burping, changing, and settling the baby back to sleep. This limits her need to get up and move, which is crucial for C-section recovery.
*   **Manage the environment:** Keep water, snacks, and any needed supplies within her reach. You can handle all diaper changes and swaddling.
*   **Be the gatekeeper of rest:** The first two weeks are a key time for health and support. Your role is to ensure she gets uninterrupted sleep between feeds. This kind of practical and emotional support from partners is a vital part of high-quality postnatal care.

Remember, your support is not just about tasks; it’s about creating a calm space where she feels safe to recover. You are both learning together, and your active presence makes a huge difference.

Schedules and place of postnatal care 
contacts
Routine postnatal care services provide a delivery 
platform for care of healthy women and their healthy 
newborns. It is provided at different time windows, 
often by different health workers in different places 
(6). Despite its importance, coverage and quality of 
postnatal care for women and newborns tend to be 
relatively poor (12). Routine postnatal care is provided 
in outpatient settings (office or health facilities) 
or at home. Its purpose is to assess the health and 
well-being of the women and newborns, to provide 
breastfeeding and hygiene counselling, parenting 
and child health counselling and general support

**What the rules say**
Group health insurance policies must clearly list what they cover, including any sub-limits for maternity or newborn care (IRDAI-ANNEX, p. 2, 32). Maternity coverage and newborn care are not automatically included; they are specific benefits the employer chooses. The policy will also state waiting periods and exclusions (IRDAI-ANNEX, p. 2).

Regardless of your insurance, your wife is entitled to free delivery and care for the sick newborn up to one year at public health institutions under the Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram (JSSK) (INDIA-JSSK, p. 2). This includes C-section, medicines, and transport. It’s a valuable backup.

Box 3.11 WHO newborn immunization guidance and considerations (as of November 2021)
Hepatitis B vaccine
All infants should receive the first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, ideally within 24 
hours. If administration within 24 hours is not feasible, all infants should receive the birth dose during the first 
contact with health facilities, up to the time of the first primary dose series. 
If administration within 24 hours is not feasible, the birth dose can still be effective in preventing perinatal 
transmission if given within seven days, particularly within three days – although it will be somewhat less effective 
than if given within 24 hours, effectiveness declining with each passing day. Even after seven days, a late birth dose 
can be effective in preventing horizontal transmission and therefore remains beneficial. 
The birth dose should be followed by two or three additional doses to complete the primary series. Vaccination 
schedules are described in the 2017 Hepatitis B vaccines: WHO position paper (192).
Polio vaccine
In polio-endemic countries and countries at high risk for importation and subsequent spread, WHO recommends 
a bivalent oral polio vaccination (bOPV) birth dose followed by a primary series of three bOPV doses and at least 
two inactivated poliovirus (IPV) dose.
Bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG) vaccine
In countries or settings with a high incidence of TB disease and/ or leprosy, a single dose of BCG vaccine should be

since evidence shows it is beneficial. Catch-up vaccination should be done at the earliest convenient encounter

Doctors give iron and folic acid (IFA) tablets to protect both you and your baby. Without enough iron, you can develop anaemia, which makes you feel very tired and can increase the risk of complications like preterm birth or having a baby with low birth weight (WHO-ANC, p. 23). Folic acid is crucial, especially early on, to help prevent serious birth defects of the baby's brain and spine (WHO-ANC, p. xi).

Starting from the second trimester, around 14-16 weeks, taking one IFA tablet daily for at least 100 days is a standard preventive measure to keep your blood healthy (MOHFW-ANC, p. 25). If you are already anaemic, your doctor will prescribe a higher dose to correct it (MOHFW-ANC, p. 80). It's common to experience mild side effects like nausea or black stools. You can try taking the tablet after a meal or at night to help with this (MOHFW-ANC, p. 25). Eating iron-rich foods like green leafy vegetables, lentils, and jaggery also helps (MOHFW-ANC, p. 24).

output.answer: I hear you, and back pain can be really draining. I can’t tell you which painkiller or dose to take, because that decision must come from your doctor who knows your full health history and pregnancy. What I can share from trusted sources is that standard care for back pain in pregnancy often includes rest, hot or cold compresses, and paracetamol (WHO-ANC, p. 81). The evidence on paracetamol for this is very low-certainty, from small studies (WHO-ANC, p. 81). There is also moderate-certainty evidence that specific exercises may help improve pain and function (WHO-ANC, p. 81). Please speak with your doctor about what is safest for you and your baby right now. They can guide you on whether any medicine is appropriate and at what dose. You might also ask them about gentle exercises or support belts, as these are mentioned in the guidance.

In a private hospital, the process is usually straightforward because the hospital itself is responsible for reporting the birth. Under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, the medical officer in charge of the hospital (or someone they authorise) must give the birth information to the local registrar (INDIA-CRS, p. 3). So, the first step is to check with the hospital's administrative desk or nursing station—they will tell you what forms they need from you and when they will send the report.

Once the hospital reports it, the birth is registered with the local registrar, who is an official appointed for your municipal or panchayat area (INDIA-CRS, p. 2). You will then need to collect the official birth certificate from that registrar's office. The hospital discharge slip you received will have all the baby's details, which is helpful for this (MOHFW-ANC, p. 119).

This certificate is a vital legal document for your child's future, like school admission, so it's important to get it done (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62). If you haven't added the baby's name yet, you can provide it to the registrar later, and they will update the record (INDIA-CRS, p. 4).

output.answer: In Tamil families, **Seemantham** and **Valaikappu** are often celebrated together, but they have different focuses. **Valaikappu** is the bangle ceremony, where married women place colourful glass bangles on the mother-to-be's wrists and bless her. The sound of the bangles is believed to soothe the baby. **Seemantham** is a pooja, more common in some families like Brahmin communities, where Vedic chants are recited for the wellbeing of the mother and baby. Often, the day includes both: the pooja and the bangle ceremony, followed by blessings, aarti, and light-hearted games. Customs vary between communities and families, so it is best to ask your family elders what they follow. For food safety during the celebration, you can check with Nestling's Nourish or your doctor.

Congratulations on your new arrival! Here is the key paperwork to focus on now.

**1. Birth Registration**
This is the most important legal document for your child's future, needed for school admission and more (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62). The hospital usually reports the birth, but you must follow up with your local registrar (often at the municipal or panchayat office) to get the official birth certificate. If you haven't chosen a name yet, you can add it later with the registrar (INDIA-CRS, p. 4).

**2. Vaccination Card**
Before your wife and baby are discharged, the hospital will give the baby's first vaccinations. Make sure you receive the vaccination card and keep it safe, as you'll need it for all future immunizations.

**3. Discharge Summary**
The hospital should provide a discharge slip with details of the delivery, the baby's condition, and advice for follow-up care (MOHFW-ANC, p. 119). Keep this for your records and for your next doctor's visit.

As a new father, you can take the lead on registering the birth and safely filing all these documents. This is a practical and loving way to support your family right now.

claims.claim: Birth registration is the most important legal document for your child's future, needed for school admission and more (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62).
The hospital usually reports the birth, but you must follow up with your local registrar (often at the municipal or panchayat office) to get the official birth certificate.
If you haven't chosen a name yet, you can add it later with the registrar (INDIA-CRS, p. 4).
Before your wife and baby are discharged, the hospital will give the baby's first vaccinations.
Make sure you receive the vaccination card and keep it safe, as you'll need it for all future immunizations.
The hospital should provide a discharge slip with details of the delivery, the baby's condition, and advice for follow-up care (MOHFW-ANC, p. 119).
Keep this for your records and for your next doctor's visit.

birth. This helps to prevent the baby from developing allergies and intolerance to other 
foods.

to reduce the severity of any infection the baby might have.

According to the Government of India's guidelines, you should have at least four antenatal check-ups during your pregnancy (MOHFW-ANC, p. 10). The suggested schedule is:

*   **1st visit:** Within the first 12 weeks, which is right now. This is for registration and your first check-up.
*   **2nd visit:** Between 14 and 26 weeks.
*   **3rd visit:** Between 28 and 34 weeks.
*   **4th visit:** Between 36 weeks and your due date.

It's wonderful that you are already thinking about this. The World Health Organization now recommends a schedule with even more contacts, suggesting eight visits throughout pregnancy for a positive experience (WHO-ANC, p. 105).

Please remember, these four visits are a minimum. Your doctor or nurse may advise you to come more often based on your specific health needs (MOHFW-ANC, p. 10). The most important thing is to get started with your first visit now for a healthy journey ahead.

Introduction 
Under-nutrition remains a pervasive issue for many women in India, with 
every third woman being undernourished and every second woman 
suffering from anaemia. This nutritional deficit often leads to an 
undernourished mother giving birth to a low birth weight baby, a condition 
that begins in -utero and whose largely irreversible effects can extend 
throughout the life cycle. Exacerbating these health challenges, economic 
and social distress compels many women to continue working right up to 
the advanced stages o f pregnancy and to prematurely resume work after 
childbirth. This sustained labour prevents their bodies from fully recovering 
and impedes their ability to exclusively breastfeed their infants during the 
crucial first six months. 
In response to these critical challenges, the Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana 
Yojana (PMMVY), a maternity benefit programme, was launched on the 1st 
January 2017. The scheme is implemented by the Ministry of Women and 
Child Development and forms a key component  of the Government of 
India's 'Mission Shakti' for women's empowerment.  
Under the 'Samarthya' sub -scheme, PMMVY focuses on economic 
empowerment and holistic development of women. It provides financial 
support to pregnant and lactating mothers under the National Food Security 
Act, 2013, to improve their health and nutrition and compensate for wage 
loss. In April 2022, PMMVY 2.0 extended maternity benefits for the second 
living child, if a girl, and to promote positive attitudes towards girls and 
improve the Sex Ratio at Birth . Mission Shakti guidelines support PMMVY 
2.0 implementation across national, state, and district levels.1

It’s wonderful that you’re thinking about this. As a father, your presence is a powerful form of support. Given your long hours, I’d suggest prioritising the visits that involve key assessments and planning.

The most important one to attend is the **third-trimester visit around 28–34 weeks**. The guidelines specifically advise the pregnant woman to see the doctor at this time, as it’s a period for a detailed check-up and to plan for the birth (MOHFW-ANC, p. 10). If you can manage one more, the **visit at 36 weeks** is also crucial. This is when you finalise the birth plan, confirm the facility, and review danger signs together (MOHFW-ANC, p. 115) (MOHFW-ANC, p. 116).

For the other visits, you can support her by ensuring she has transport, reviewing the reports she brings home, and simply listening. Your calm involvement makes a real difference.

Yes, the tetanus vaccination is recommended for all pregnant women in India to protect you and your baby from neonatal tetanus (WHO-ANC, p. 70). The guidelines you'll follow in India use the Tetanus Toxoid (TT) vaccine, which is part of the national schedule (MOHFW-ANC, p. 108).

The standard schedule is two doses. You should get the first dose as early as possible in pregnancy, and the second dose four weeks later, and at least two weeks before your due date (MOHFW-ANC, p. 26) (WHO-ANC, p. 70). If you received two TT doses in a previous pregnancy within the last three years, you would only need one booster dose this time (MOHFW-ANC, p. 26).

Evidence shows that at least two doses are highly effective, reducing neonatal tetanus deaths by about 94% (WHO-ANC, p. 71). The injection is given in your upper arm, and you might have some mild soreness or redness for a day or two, which is normal (MOHFW-ANC, p. 26). Please discuss your vaccination history with your doctor or ANM at your next visit to get the right dose for you.

RECOMMENDATION C.5: T etanus toxoid vaccination is recommended for all pregnant women, 
depending on previous tetanus vaccination exposure, to prevent neonatal mortality from 
tetanus. (Recommended)
Remarks
• This recommendation is consistent with recommendations from the 2006 WHO guideline on Maternal 
immunization against tetanus (134). The GDG endorses the 2006 guideline approach, which recommends 
the following.
 – If a pregnant woman has not previously been vaccinated, or if her immunization status is unknown, 
she should receive two doses of a tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine (TT-CV) one month apart with 
the second dose given at least two weeks before delivery. T wo doses protect against tetanus infection 
for 1–3 years in most people. A third dose is recommended six months after the second dose, which 
should extend protection to at least five years.

given after the third dose, in the two subsequent years or during two subsequent pregnancies.
 – If a woman has had 1–4 doses of a TT-CV in the past, she should receive one dose of a TT-CV during 
each subsequent pregnancy to a total of five doses (five doses protects throughout the childbearing 
years).
• T etanus vaccination and clean delivery practices are major components of the strategy to eradicate 
maternal and neonatal tetanus globally (147).
• Effective surveillance is critical for identifying areas or populations at high risk of neonatal tetanus and for 
monitoring the impact of interventions.
• A monitoring system should include an immunization register, personal vaccination cards and maternal 
health records, which should be held by the woman.
• For effective implementation, ANC health-care providers need to be trained in tetanus vaccination and 
the vaccine, equipment and supplies (refrigerator, needles and syringes) need to be readily available at

• A healthy diet contains adequate energy, protein, vitamins and minerals, obtained through the

overweight and obesity, depending on resources and women’s preferences. Interventions should be

maintaining a good level of fitness throughout pregnancy, without trying to reach peak fitness level or

That's a very helpful question. Think of them as two different types of care that often happen at the same time, especially around the 6-week mark.

A **paediatrician visit** is a full check-up on your baby's overall health and development. The doctor will examine your baby, check their weight gain, ask about breastfeeding, and look for any signs of illness (MOHFW-ANC, p. 68). It's a chance for you to ask any questions you have about caring for your baby.

An **immunisation appointment** is specifically for giving vaccines, as per the Universal Immunisation Programme (MOHFW-ANC, p. 68). The focus is on protecting your baby from serious diseases.

Often, these two happen together. The guidelines recommend a postnatal contact during week six after birth, which is when a transition to well-infant care and referrals for infant immunisation usually occur (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 152). So, your baby's 6-week visit might include both a full check-up by the paediatrician and their scheduled vaccines. You can always ask your doctor what to expect at each appointment.

RECOMMENDATION 44
A minimum of four postnatal care contacts is recommended. 
If birth is in a health facility, healthy women and newborns should receive postnatal care in the facility for 
at least 24 hours after birth. If birth is at home, the first postnatal contact should be as early as possible 
within 24 hours of birth. At least three additional postnatal contacts are recommended for healthy

• The number, timing and content of postnatal care contacts should be tailored to each woman’s and 
newborn’s health outcomes and needs, and guided by the recommendations in this guideline, including:

 – the skills and confidence of the woman to care for herself and the skills and confidence of parents/
caregivers/family to care for the newborn; 
 – the home environment and other factors that may influence the ability to provide care for the woman 
and newborn in the home, and care-seeking behaviour; and
 – the place of birth and the time of discharge from the health facility for a facility-based birth. 
• In making this recommendation, the Guideline Development Group considered the following. 
 – There was insufficient evidence from randomized controlled trials on the effects of more frequent 
postnatal care contacts compared with less frequent contacts.

birth, in particular on the day of birth, with another increase during the second week after birth.

caregivers and the organization of services as per the health system.

1 Introduction
1.1 Background
An imaging ultrasound scan is widely used to estimate gestational age, investigate suspected pregnancy 
complications and monitor complicated pregnancies when they occur. In 2016, the World Health Organization 
(WHO) added a single ultrasound scan before 24 weeks of pregnancy to its list of recommended interventions 
for routine antenatal care (ANC) (1). In most high-income countries, routine antenatal ultrasound screening has 
been standard practice for some time, often being conducted in both the first and second trimesters (2). When 
conducted in the first trimester (up to and including 13 weeks and 6 days of gestation), an imaging ultrasound 
scan is aimed at confirming fetal viability, identifying the location of the gestational sac, establishing gestational 
age, determining the number of fetuses and, in the presence of a multiple pregnancy, assessing chorionicity and 
amnionicity; also, towards the end of the first trimester, nuchal translucency thickness is commonly measured 
in settings that offer screening for fetal chromosomal abnormalities (3). Second-trimester ultrasound scans 
conducted between 18 and 24 weeks allow for more detailed examination of fetal anatomy and detection of fetal 
anomalies, provide information on the number of fetuses present, identify the location of the placenta and enable 
an estimate of gestational age (4). 
A 2015 systematic review on ultrasound scans before 24 weeks of pregnancy (5) and a qualitative review on 
women’s views and experiences of pregnancy (6) informed the 2016 WHO recommendations on antenatal 
care for a positive pregnancy experience (1). The ultrasound recommendation (B2.4) is: “One ultrasound scan 
before 24 weeks of gestation (early ultrasound) is recommended for pregnant women to estimate gestational 
age, improve detection of fetal anomalies and multiple pregnancies, reduce induction of labour for post-
term pregnancy, and improve a woman’s pregnancy experience.” In the context of a new cluster-randomized 
randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluating the impact of routine ultrasound scans in low-resource settings (7), 
an independent Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) prioritized updating the 2016 recommendation. A new 
systematic review on routine ultrasound before 24 weeks of pregnancy has since been conducted (8).

address the guideline’s PICO question).

It’s a good idea to have your bag ready by about 36 weeks, or earlier if your doctor has mentioned a chance of early birth. Here’s what to pack, based on Nestling’s checklist and trusted guidelines.

**Documents**
- Your Mother and Child Protection (MCP) card, all antenatal records, scan and test reports.
- Photo ID and address proof for you and the person going with you (common practice).
- Health insurance card or policy number, and the hospital’s pre-authorisation form if you have one (common practice).
- If you’re using JSY at an accredited private hospital, the BPL or SC/ST certificate where your state requires it.

**For you**
- Clean, loose, front-opening clothes that have been washed and sun-dried—these make breastfeeding easier.
- Maternity pads or clean cloth.
- Food and water for yourself and your support person.
- Toiletries, slippers, a shawl or sweater, and a phone charger (common practice).

**For your baby**
- Clean towels or soft cloth to dry and wrap the baby.
- Clean baby clothes, washed andus a cap and socks to keep the baby warm.

**Plan ahead**
- Know which facility you’ll go to and how to reach it.
- Arrange transport and save the ambulance number (108; 102 for free transport to a government hospital).
- Keep an emergency fund and know which schemes like JSY or JSSK can help with costs.
- Decide who will go with you and who will look after home and children.

You’re doing wonderfully preparing for your baby’s arrival. Packing this bag is a loving, practical step you can take now.

output.answer: Yes, you can drink coffee, but it's wise to keep your daily caffeine intake low. The WHO recommends that pregnant women with a high daily caffeine intake (more than 300 mg per day) should lower it to reduce the risk of pregnancy loss and low birth weight (WHO-ANC, p. 38). Remember, caffeine is also in tea, cola drinks, and chocolate (WHO-ANC, p. 38).

unsupported: A cup of instant coffee has about 50–65 mg of caffeine, while brewed coffee can have 80–120 mg.
One small cup a day is generally fine, but try to stay well below the 300 mg limit.
It's best to avoid tea or coffee for at least one hour before and after meals, as they can interfere with iron absorption from your food.
Your doctor will guide you on iron and folic acid supplements, which are important now.

claims.claim: You can drink coffee while pregnant, but it's wise to keep your daily caffeine intake low.
The WHO recommends that pregnant women with a high daily caffeine intake (more than 300 mg per day) should lower it to reduce the risk of pregnancy loss and low birth weight.
Caffeine is also in tea, cola drinks, and chocolate.

output.answer: I'd like to help. Could you tell me a little more: what you're noticing or wondering about, and how many weeks along you are (or how old your baby is)?

Yes, walking every day is a wonderful way to stay active during your pregnancy. The WHO recommends that pregnant women keep physically active to stay healthy and prevent excessive weight gain (WHO-ANC, p. 15). Walking is a safe, low-impact activity with minimal risk of losing your balance, which is exactly the kind of exercise suggested (WHO-ANC, p. 15).

At 22 weeks, you are likely starting to feel your baby's movements, which is a reassuring sign of well-being (MOHFW-ANC, p. 23). While you walk, simply enjoy this connection. There is no need for formal kick-counting right now; just be aware of your baby's pattern of movement. If you ever notice a significant decrease in movements, you should contact your doctor (WHO-ANC, p. 54).

Listen to your body, stay hydrated, and avoid getting overheated. The goal is to maintain a good level of fitness, not to push yourself to exhaustion (WHO-ANC, p. 15). Keep up the great work, and enjoy your daily walks.

Box 3.11 WHO newborn immunization guidance and considerations (as of November 2021)
Hepatitis B vaccine
All infants should receive the first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, ideally within 24 
hours. If administration within 24 hours is not feasible, all infants should receive the birth dose during the first 
contact with health facilities, up to the time of the first primary dose series. 
If administration within 24 hours is not feasible, the birth dose can still be effective in preventing perinatal 
transmission if given within seven days, particularly within three days – although it will be somewhat less effective 
than if given within 24 hours, effectiveness declining with each passing day. Even after seven days, a late birth dose 
can be effective in preventing horizontal transmission and therefore remains beneficial. 
The birth dose should be followed by two or three additional doses to complete the primary series. Vaccination 
schedules are described in the 2017 Hepatitis B vaccines: WHO position paper (192).
Polio vaccine
In polio-endemic countries and countries at high risk for importation and subsequent spread, WHO recommends 
a bivalent oral polio vaccination (bOPV) birth dose followed by a primary series of three bOPV doses and at least 
two inactivated poliovirus (IPV) dose.
Bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG) vaccine
In countries or settings with a high incidence of TB disease and/ or leprosy, a single dose of BCG vaccine should be 
given to neonates at birth, or as soon as possible thereafter, for prevention of TB and leprosy. If it cannot be given 
at birth, it should be given at the earliest opportunity thereafter and should not be delayed.
If the birth dose was missed, catch-up vaccination of unvaccinated older infants and children is recommended 
since evidence shows it is beneficial. Catch-up vaccination should be done at the earliest convenient encounter 
with the health system to minimize known or unknown exposure to TB- or leprosy-infected contacts.

It is good you are thinking about this now. The general advice is to have your hospital bag packed by about **36 weeks** of pregnancy. If your doctor has mentioned any reason you might deliver earlier, you should pack it sooner.

Here is a simple checklist to help you prepare, based on trusted Indian guidelines:

**Documents**
- Your Mother and Child Protection (MCP) card, all antenatal records, scan and test reports
- Photo ID and address proof for you and the person going with you (common_practice)
- Health insurance card or policy number, and the hospital's pre-authorisation form if you have one (common_practice)

**For You**
- Clean, loose, front-opening clothes for breastfeeding
- Maternity pads or clean cloth
- Food and water for you and your support person
- Toiletries, slippers, a shawl or sweater, phone charger (common_practice)

**For the Baby**
- Clean towels or soft cloth to dry and wrap the baby
- Clean baby clothes, a cap and socks, all washed and sun-dried

**Plan Ahead**
- Know which facility you will go to and how to reach it.
- Save the ambulance number (108; 102 for free transport to a government hospital).
- Decide who will go with you and who will look after home and children.

You have plenty of time to gather these things calmly. Is there anything else you would like to know about preparing for the birth?

claims.claim: The general advice is to have your hospital bag packed by about 36 weeks of pregnancy.
If your doctor has mentioned any reason you might deliver earlier, you should pack it sooner.
Your Mother and Child Protection (MCP) card, all antenatal records, scan and test reports should be in the hospital bag.
Photo ID and address proof for you and the person going with you should be included.
Health insurance card or policy number, and the hospital's pre-authorisation form if you have one should be included.
Clean, loose, front-opening clothes for breastfeeding should be packed.
Maternity pads or clean cloth should be packed.
Food and water for you and your support person should be included.
Toiletries, slippers, a shawl or sweater, phone charger should be included.
Clean towels or soft cloth to dry and wrap the baby should be packed.
Clean baby clothes, a cap and socks, all washed and sun-dried should be packed.
Know which facility you will go to and how to reach it.
Save the ambulance number (108; 102 for free transport to a government hospital).
Decide who will go with you and who will look after home and children.

A.2: Iron and folic acid supplements
A.2.1: Daily iron and folic acid supplements
RECOMMENDATION A.2.1: Daily oral iron and folic acid supplementation with 30 mg to 
60 mg of elemental irona and 400 µg (0.4 mg) folic acidb is recommended for pregnant 
women to prevent maternal anaemia, puerperal sepsis, low birth weight, and preterm birth.c 
(Recommended)
Remarks
• This recommendation supersedes the 2012 WHO Guideline: daily iron and folic acid supplementation in 
pregnant women (36) and should be considered alongside Recommendation A.2.2 on intermittent iron.
• In settings where anaemia in pregnant women is a severe public health problem (i.e. where at least 40% 
of pregnant women have a blood haemoglobin [Hb] concentration < 110 g/L), a daily dose of 60 mg of 
elemental iron is preferred over a lower dose. 
• In the first and third trimesters, the Hb threshold for diagnosing anaemia is 110 g/L; in the second 
trimester, the threshold is 105 g/L (50). 
• If a woman is diagnosed with anaemia during pregnancy, her daily elemental iron should be increased 
to 120 mg until her Hb concentration rises to normal (Hb 110 g/L or higher) (34, 51). Thereafter, she can 
resume the standard daily antenatal iron dose to prevent recurrence of anaemia.
• Effective communication with pregnant women about diet and healthy eating – including providing 
information about food sources of vitamins and minerals, and dietary diversity – is an integral part of 
preventing anaemia and providing quality ANC. 
• Effective communication strategies are vital for improving the acceptability of, and adherence to, 
supplementation schemes. 
• Stakeholders may need to consider ways of reminding pregnant women to take their supplements and of 
assisting them to manage associated side-effects.
• In areas with endemic infections that may cause anaemia through blood loss, increased red cell 
destruction or decreased red cell production, such as malaria and hookworm, measures to prevent, 
diagnose and treat these infections should be implemented.

A.3: Calcium supplements
RECOMMENDATION A.3: In populations with low dietary calcium intake, daily calcium 
supplementation (1.5–2.0 g oral elemental calcium) is recommended for pregnant women to 
reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia. (Context-specific recommendation)
Remarks
• This recommendation is consistent with the 2011 WHO recommendations for prevention and treatment of 
pre-eclampsia and eclampsia (57) (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence) and supersedes 
the WHO recommendation found in the 2013 Guideline: calcium supplementation in pregnant women (38).
• Dietary counselling of pregnant women should promote adequate calcium intake through locally 
available, calcium-rich foods.
• Dividing the dose of calcium may improve acceptability. The suggested scheme for calcium 
supplementation is 1.5–2 g daily, with the total dose divided into three doses, preferably taken at 
mealtimes.
• Negative interactions between iron and calcium supplements may occur. Therefore, the two nutrients 
should preferably be administered several hours apart rather than concomitantly (38).
• As there is no clear evidence on the timing of initiation of calcium supplementation, stakeholders may 
wish to commence supplementation at the first ANC visit, given the possibility of compliance issues.
• T o reach the most vulnerable populations and ensure a timely and continuous supply of supplements, 
stakeholders may wish to consider task shifting the provision of calcium supplementation in community 
settings with poor access to health-care professionals (see Recommendation E.6.1, in section E: Health 
systems interventions to improve the utilization and quality of ANC).
• The implementation and impact of this recommendation should be monitored at the health service, 
regional and country levels, based on clearly defined criteria and indicators associated with locally agreed 
targets. Successes and failures should be evaluated to inform integration of this recommendation into the 
ANC package.

In pregnancy, severe anaemia is 
associated with an increased risk of maternal and 
infant mortality (34). It is estimated that about half of 
the anaemia found in pregnant women is amenable 
to iron supplementation (33); however, this may 
be quite variable and is likely to be much lower in 
malaria-endemic areas.
In addition to causing anaemia, iron deficiency 
adversely affects the use of energy sources by 
muscles and, thus, physical capacity and work 
performance, and also adversely affects immune 
status and morbidity from infections (35). Folate 
(vitamin B9) deficiency, in addition to anaemia it is 
also linked to fetal neural tube defects (36). Vitamin A 
deficiency affects about 19 million pregnant women, 
mostly in Africa and South-East Asia, causing night 
blindness (37).
Calcium deficiency is associated with an increased 
risk of pre-eclampsia (38), and deficiencies of other 
vitamins and minerals, such as vitamin E, C, B6 and 
zinc, have also been postulated to play a role in 
pre-eclampsia. Zinc deficiency is associated with 
impaired immunity (39). Vitamin C intake enhances 
iron absorption from the gut; however, zinc, iron 
and other mineral supplements may compete 
for absorption, and it is unclear whether such 
interactions have health consequences (39).
For the ANC guideline, the GDG evaluated the 
evidence on various vitamin and mineral supplements 
that might theoretically lead to improved maternal 
and perinatal outcomes. In addition, as both 
undernourishment and overnourishment may have 
negative consequences for pregnant women and 
their babies, the GDG also evaluated evidence on 
the effects of various dietary interventions to reduce 
the impact of these conditions. Caffeine is possibly 
the most widely used psychoactive substance in the 
world (40), and the GDG also evaluated evidence 
on the impact, if any, of caffeine restriction during 
pregnancy.
